unit.title: 2D Shapes
unit.blurb: Properties of quadrilaterals, the parts of a circle, and rotational symmetry.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Identify, describe, classify and sketch quadrilaterals, including trapezia and kites, using their properties.

O2.t: Know the parts of a circle: centre, radius, diameter and circumference.

O3.t: Identify rotational symmetry in familiar shapes and find the order of rotational symmetry.

p: At a kite festival, children make kites from four sticks of wood. Some kites look like squares, some like rhombuses and some like real 'kite' shapes.
What makes each four-sided shape different? Think about sides, angles and diagonals before you read on.
A quadrilateral has 4 straight sides and 4 angles that add to 360°.

p: A **square** is a special rectangle (and a special rhombus). A **rectangle** and a **rhombus** are special parallelograms.
So 'every square is a rectangle' is **true**, but 'every rectangle is a square' is **false**.
Use the properties to identify shapes – not how they look when turned.

p: A groundskeeper paints the **centre circle** on a football pitch. She ties a 9.15 m rope to a peg in the middle and walks round.
Why does this make a perfect circle? How wide is the circle? Think about it before you read on.
Every point on a circle is the **same distance** from the **centre**. That distance is the **radius** (r).
The **diameter** (d) goes right across through the centre: **d = 2 × r**. The distance all the way round is the **circumference**.
Pitch circle: r = 9.15 m, so d = **18.3 m**.
Use **compasses**: open them to the radius using a ruler, put the point on the centre, and turn carefully without changing the width.
To draw a circle with a given diameter, halve it first to get the radius.

lesson.t: How do I draw and measure circles?
p: Step 1: Mark the centre.
Step 2: Set the compasses to the radius (half the diameter).
Step 3: Turn the compasses all the way round.
Step 4: Check: every diameter you draw should be 2 × radius.

p: A paper windmill has **4 identical blades**. As it spins, it keeps looking exactly the same at certain moments.
How many times does it look the same in one full turn? Think about it before you read on.
A full turn is 360°; a quarter turn is 90°.
A shape has **rotational symmetry** if it looks exactly the same **more than once** as it turns through a full turn about its centre.
The **order** of rotational symmetry is how many times it fits onto itself in one full turn. The windmill: **order 4**.
Trace the shape, put a pencil point on the centre, and turn the paper. Count how many times the tracing fits exactly, up to a full turn.
Every shape fits once after a full turn, so **order 1 means no rotational symmetry**.

qq.prompt: Order of rotational symmetry of a regular pentagon?

lesson.t: How do I find the order of rotational symmetry?
p: Step 1: Find the centre of the shape.
Step 2: Turn it (or a tracing) slowly through a full turn.
Step 3: Count how many times it looks exactly the same.
Step 4: Order 1 means no rotational symmetry.

steps: looks the same after a half turn
